title: 1-bit and 2-bit Characters
statement: An alphabet has two kinds of characters: a one-bit character written as `0`, and a two-bit character written as either `10` or `11`. The binary array `bits` is a message made of such characters placed back to back, and its last element is always `0`. Read from the start, the message splits into characters in exactly one way. Return `true` if the final character of that split is the one-bit character, and `false` if it is a two-bit character.
notes:
## Intuition

Because no character's code is the beginning of another's, the message can be decoded greedily from the left: a `1` always starts a two-bit character and a `0` at a character boundary is always a one-bit character. So simply walk the message one character at a time and see where the last character begins. If a character starts exactly at the final index, it is the lone `0`; if the walk jumps over the final index, the last `0` was the second half of a two-bit character.

## Approach

1. Let `last` be the index of the final bit and start `i` at 0, the start of the first character.
2. While `i` is before `last`: a `1` at `i` begins a two-bit character, so add 2; a `0` is a whole character, so add 1.
3. When the loop stops, `i` is either `last` (a character starts on the final bit) or `last + 1` (the final bit was swallowed). Return `i === last`.

## Example 1, step by step

`bits = [1, 0, 0]`, so `last = 2`. At `i = 0` the bit is `1`, a two-bit character `10`, so `i` becomes 2. Now `i < last` is false and the loop ends. `i === last`, so a character begins on the final `0` and the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each step moves `i` forward by at least one.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Looking only at the bit before the last one is wrong: in `[1, 1, 0]` it is a `1`, yet that `1` belongs to `11` and the final `0` stands alone.
- Stop the loop at `last`, not at `bits.length`, otherwise every message ends past the end.
- A message of a single `[0]` never enters the loop and must return `true`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `last` | index of the final bit |
| `i` | index where the next character starts |

narration.2: Remember the index of the final bit, which is always 0.
narration.3: The first character starts at index 0.
narration.5: Keep decoding while the next character starts before the final bit.
narration.6: A 1 can only begin a two-bit character...
narration.8: A 0 at a character boundary is a whole one-bit character.
narration.12: If a character starts exactly on the final bit, that last character is the lone 0.
